latvian gambit.intro: We're playing the white side of the Latvian Gambit, a sharp and unsound opening where Black pushes the f-pawn early, weakening their kingside. Our plan is to open the center and exploit the exposed king with simple, forceful moves.
latvian gambit.shortIntro: White punishes Black's early f5 with central play and direct threats.
latvian gambit.outro: By opening the center and targeting the weak f7 square, we've built a winning attack. Simple development and concrete tactics are all it takes to refute the Latvian Gambit.

ideas.text: Bc4 develops the bishop to a powerful diagonal, eyeing f7—the weakest square in Black's camp. This move increases pressure and threatens immediate checkmate if Black isn't careful.

ideas.text: fxe4 captures your e4 pawn, but Black's king is now even more exposed. Instead of recapturing automatically, we look for a more forceful continuation.

ideas.text: Nxe5 sacrifices the knight temporarily, but it opens the e5 square for your queen. This is a classic idea: trade on e5 to deliver a devastating check on h5.
ideas.shortText: Nxe5 opens lines.

ideas.text: Qg5 is Black's attempt to defend f7 and counterattack, but it leaves the queen misplaced. We now have a powerful follow-up: Nf7 forks the queen and rook.
ideas.shortText: Qg5 is a poor square.

ideas.text: Nf7 forks Black's queen and rook, winning material. This knight jump is the direct punishment for Black's careless play—the queen must move, and we'll capture the rook.
ideas.shortText: Nf7 forks queen and rook.

ideas.text: Qxg2 — Black ignores the fork, snapping off a pawn and attacking the rook on h1. It looks scary, but the queen has wandered far from her own king, and your fork on f7 still wins the exchange. Defend calmly and the counterplay evaporates.
ideas.shortText: Qxg2 ignores the fork and attacks the rook on h1.

ideas.text: Rf1 is a quiet but essential move. It gets the rook off the back rank and prepares to join the attack, while also defending the f2 pawn. Black's king is still exposed, and we want to bring all our pieces into the game.
ideas.shortText: Rf1 brings the rook into play.

ideas.text: d5 is a desperate attempt by Black to block the diagonal and gain space. But it doesn't solve the king's safety issues. We can simply continue our development, as Black's position remains full of holes.
ideas.shortText: d5 doesn't fix Black's problems.

ideas.text: Nxh8 collects the cornered rook. The knight may take a few moves to find its way out of h8, but the material is decisive and Black's king remains the one in real danger.
ideas.shortText: Nxh8 collects the rook in the corner.

ideas.text: Nf6 is a final blunder, but the game is already lost. Black's knight moves to f6, but it doesn't defend anything crucial. We can now finish with a simple tactic, like Qe2+ followed by Rd1, winning the queen.
ideas.shortText: Nf6 is a decisive mistake.

four knights game glek system.intro: Welcome to the Four Knights Game: Glek System. This is an underrated weapon that sets up a fianchetto against Black's king pawn setup. Let's walk through the first critical moves.
four knights game glek system.shortIntro: Glek System: fianchetto the bishop to fight for the center.
four knights game glek system.outro: After Nxd5, Black has central control but White's fianchettoed bishop and flexible setup offer dynamic chances. The key ideas are to complete kingside development and prepare either d4 or f4 breaks.

ideas.text: Nxc3. Black trades knights, capturing on c3. This is a common decision in the Glek; we should be happy to recapture with the b-pawn, as it opens the b-file and prepares d2-d4.
ideas.shortText: Nxc3 trades knights, leading to doubled pawns for us.

ideas.text: bxc3. We recapture with the b-pawn, accepting doubled pawns. This structure is intentional: it opens the b-file for our rook and makes it easier to push d4, gaining central control. The doubled pawns are not a weakness here—they give us dynamic play.
ideas.shortText: bxc3 opens the b-file and prepares d4.

elephant gambit.intro: We're playing the white side of the Elephant Gambit. Black's second move d5 is a sharp gambit, but we can handle it with precise play. Let's walk through the critical line.
elephant gambit.shortIntro: White's response to the Elephant Gambit.
elephant gambit.outro: With Qg5, Black's queen enters the game early. We have a strong position with better development and central control. Stay alert for tactics.

sicilian defense grand prix attack.intro: We're playing the Grand Prix Attack — White's ferocious answer to the Sicilian, and the whole story aims at one square: f7. We'll brace the centre, launch the f-pawn, point the bishop at f7 and swing the queen toward h4, ripping open the f-file before Black's queenside counterplay ever arrives. Watch how every move feeds that single plan.
sicilian defense grand prix attack.shortIntro: The Grand Prix: White's kingside storm aimed at f7.
sicilian defense grand prix attack.outro: With f4, White has committed to the Grand Prix structure — the bishop will go to c4, the queen will eye h4, and the attack on f7 begins. Black now needs to choose a setup: fianchetto with g6, or play e6/d6 to keep the center solid. The battle lines are drawn.

ideas.text: e4 opens the game and stakes a claim in the center — the first step in any aggressive Sicilian setup. White immediately signals that this won't be a quiet positional game.
ideas.shortText: e4 claims central space and starts the fight.

ideas.text: c5 is Black's classic Sicilian response, immediately challenging White's center from the flank. It prevents White from building a big pawn duo with d4 and sets up an asymmetrical struggle where Black will counterattack on the queenside or in the center.
ideas.shortText: c5 challenges the center and starts Sicilian counterplay.

ideas.text: Nc3 does double duty: it defends e4 so Black can't strike there for free, and it keeps the knight off f3 for now, letting White decide which attacking setup to build. This is the hallmark of the Grand Prix — White delays d4 to avoid opening lines for Black's pieces.
ideas.shortText: Nc3 defends e4 and keeps options open.

ideas.text: Nc6 is Black's most flexible move here — it develops a piece without committing to a specific pawn structure. Black waits to see where White puts the bishop before deciding whether to play d6, e6, or g6. This keeps Black ready to respond to White's plan.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 develops and waits for White's bishop.

ideas.text: f4 is the defining move of the Grand Prix Attack. White immediately starts building a kingside pawn storm, planning to follow up with Bc4 (or Bb5) and Qe1-h4. The idea is to rip open the f-file and deliver checkmate before Black can organize counterplay. Black must now choose a solid setup — the most common are g6 (fianchetto) or e6/d6 (classical).
ideas.shortText: f4 launches the kingside attack; Black must respond carefully.

bird opening.intro: Welcome to the Bird Opening. White starts with a flank pawn push, aiming to control e5 and develop quickly. Black responds by occupying the center with d5, a solid reply.
bird opening.shortIntro: Bird Opening: f4, d5, Nf3, g6, g3, Bg7, Bg2, Nf6, O-O, O-O.
bird opening.outro: Both sides have castled, reaching a typical position from the Bird Opening. White has a flexible setup with the fianchettoed bishop, while Black has solid development. The game is balanced, with plans involving central breaks like e5 or c5.

sicilian defense taimanov variation.intro: We're stepping into the Sicilian Taimanov, a flexible and solid system for Black. The key ideas are controlling the center with e6 and developing harmoniously, aiming for a strong pawn structure and active piece play.
sicilian defense taimanov variation.shortIntro: Sicilian Taimanov: solid, flexible, and ready to counterattack.
sicilian defense taimanov variation.outro: That's the Taimanov setup. Black has a solid structure and good development, ready for a strategic middlegame.

Nb5.text: You know this road well — everything up to here is the Taimanov you've already mastered. The main line plays Nc3, keeping the center solid and preparing the familiar dance where your queen comes to c7 and Ndb5 knocks it back. Today's sideline, Nb5, is a different beast: the knight jumps in eyeing the d6 square, and you calmly take that square away with d6. White grabs space with c4, and only after a6 does the knight concede the trip to a3, where it sits on the rim. That wandering costs time — you develop freely and castle, and the fight becomes piece activity against White's space rather than the usual central tension.

rubinstein opening.intro: We're playing the Rubinstein Opening, a solid and flexible system. The key is to build a strong pawn center and develop pieces harmoniously, preparing for a kingside attack.
rubinstein opening.shortIntro: Rubinstein Opening: build center, develop, attack.
rubinstein opening.outro: With this setup, we've established a firm grip on the center and good piece coordination. Now we can look to castle and continue with our plans, keeping an eye on Black's counterplay.

queen s pawn game colle system.intro: This is the Colle System, a setup where White builds a solid, harmonious position before striking in the center. queen s pawn game colle system.shortIntro: The Colle System: White builds a solid center to fight for e5.
queen s pawn game colle system.outro: With both kings castled, the stage is set. White's pieces are perfectly placed to support the e4 break or a kingside attack, while Black's setup is solid but passive. The battle for the center and the initiative is just beginning.

sicilian defense alapin variation.shortIntro: The Alapin: claim the center with c3 and dare Black to react.

d5.label: Barmen Defense
d5.teaser: d5 — Black strikes at the center immediately, turning the Alapin into a kind of Scandi with the c-pawns still on the board. The queen will come out early, and that's both a strength and a target.
d5.shortTeaser: d5 — Black challenges the center; the queen will be a target.

ideas.text: exd5 — We take the pawn, and Black's queen recaptures on d5. That queen is a powerful piece, but it's also a magnet — every move we make from here will be aimed at chasing it around and using its exposure to build our initiative.
ideas.shortText: exd5 — Black's queen comes out early; we'll chase it.

ideas.text: Qxd5 — There she is, the queen on d5. She controls a lot of squares, but she's also a target. Our whole plan is to develop with tempo, hitting that queen, and if Black mishandles it, the initiative will be ours.
ideas.shortText: Qxd5 — The queen is exposed; we'll develop with tempo.

ideas.shortText: d4 — The c3 pawn pays off; we take the center.

ideas.text: cxd4 — We recapture, and now the c3 square is free. Our knight will come to c3 next, hitting that queen on d5. The queen is already feeling the heat, and Black's early development is starting to look like a liability.
ideas.shortText: cxd4 — The c3 square is open; the knight is coming.

ideas.text: Nc6 — Black develops the knight, but the queen on d5 is still in the center. We're going to bring our knight to f3, and then we'll see how Black tries to handle the pressure. The queen's position is the key — it's both a strength and a weakness.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 — Black develops, but the queen remains a target.

ideas.shortText: Nf3 — We prepare Bc4, hitting the queen.

ideas.shortText: Bg4 — A pin, but the queen is still the target.

ideas.shortText: Nc3 — The knight hits the queen; we gain tempo.

rapport jobava system.intro: This opening is built on a single tension: White deliberately breaks the classic rule of not blocking the c-pawn, and in doing so creates a uniquely aggressive setup. The knight on c3 isn't just developing—it's a springboard for tactical ideas like Nb5, and the whole system is designed to put immediate pressure on Black's center and king. Every move here serves that story.

Instead, we'll use our pieces to pressure the center, and the knight is about to take a very un-London-like post.

This is the move that makes the Jabava London different from a passive London.

petrov s defense stafford gambit.intro: The Stafford Gambit is all about creating chaos before White can consolidate. We sacrifice a pawn to open lines and target f2, banking on White's king getting stuck in the center. Every move we make is about speed and threats—if White gets to castle, our initiative fizzles out.

sicilian defense closed.intro: This line is about choosing your battleground. Black plays the Sicilian, and instead of diving into the open main lines, we steer into the Closed Sicilian with Nc3. The story here is about controlling the center and preparing a kingside attack, while Black tries to find counterplay on the queenside or in the center. Every move we make builds toward that central tension.
sicilian defense closed.shortIntro: We choose the Closed Sicilian with Nc3, setting up a central and kingside battle.
sicilian defense closed.outro: With Nc3, we've set the stage for a closed, maneuvering battle. The center is braced, and we're ready to expand on the kingside with f4 or g3, while Black will try to undermine our center with ...d5 or ...e5. The tension is set — now it's about who breaks first.

ideas.text: We start with e4, claiming our share of the center and opening lines for the bishop and queen. This is the move that defines the Sicilian — Black's c5 will immediately challenge our central pawn, but we're ready for the fight.

ideas.text: Black plays c5, the Sicilian's signature move — a pawn thrust that fights for the d4 square and creates an unbalanced, double-edged game. This is Black's way of saying they're not interested in a quiet center; they want a fight.

ideas.text: Nc3 is our gateway to the Closed Sicilian. Instead of rushing into the open main lines with Nf3 and d4, we keep the center closed and prepare to build a kingside attack. This move also keeps Black guessing—they can't force us into their favorite theory.

d6.text: You know this road well — everything up to here is the same closed Sicilian you've walked before. The main line plays Nc6, heading straight into the Botvinnik setup where you'll fianchetto on g6 and build that solid kingside fortress. Today's sideline, d6, is the Carlsen Variation — a quieter, more flexible move that keeps the c-pawn holding the center and invites white to open things with d4. Watch how the queen comes out to d2 after the trade — that's the signal that white is aiming for a slower, more positional squeeze rather than the sharp kingside race.
d6.shortText: Nc6 heads for the Botvinnik; d6 invites the Carlsen — two different plans.

Nc6.label: Botvinnik Defense
Nc6.teaser: Nc6 keeps our Accelerated Dragon options alive — if White ever plays Nf3, we can still transpose into our favorite setup with g6.
Nc6.shortTeaser: Nc6 keeps our Accelerated Dragon options alive.

ideas.text: g3 starts the Closed Sicilian — White signals a slower, more positional fight, avoiding the sharp Open Sicilian lines. Our knight on c6 already eyes d4, and now we'll fianchetto our bishop to pressure the center from afar.
ideas.shortText: g3 begins the Closed Sicilian — a slower, positional fight.

ideas.text: g6 mirrors White's setup — we're building our own fianchetto, aiming our bishop at the long diagonal. This is the Accelerated Dragon structure we know and love, even if White chose a different path.
ideas.shortText: g6 mirrors White's fianchetto — our bishop eyes the long diagonal.

ideas.text: Bg2 completes White's kingside fianchetto — the bishop bears down on d5 and the a8-h1 diagonal. Our plan is to challenge that diagonal with our own bishop and prepare to strike in the center.
ideas.shortText: Bg2 finishes White's fianchetto — pressure on d5.

ideas.text: Bg7 develops our bishop to its ideal square, directly opposing White's bishop on the long diagonal. Now both sides are committed to a battle for control of the center and the dark squares.
ideas.shortText: Bg7 develops our bishop to oppose White's.

ideas.text: d3 supports the e4 pawn and prepares to develop the knight to e2 or f3. White is keeping the center solid before deciding on a plan. We'll respond with d6, maintaining our flexible setup.
ideas.shortText: d3 solidifies the center for White.

ideas.text: d6 reinforces our c5 pawn and prepares to develop our kingside pieces. This is the classic Sicilian move — we keep the center flexible while we finish development. Notice how our pawn chain c5-d6 controls the important d4 and e5 squares.
ideas.shortText: d6 reinforces c5 and prepares development.

ideas.text: f4 grabs space on the kingside — White is setting up a Grand Prix-like attack, planning to push f5 and maybe trade dark-squared bishops. This is the critical moment: we must respond energetically to prevent White from gaining a free hand.
ideas.shortText: f4 signals White's kingside ambitions.

ideas.text: e5 is the key break! By pushing this pawn, we challenge White's center and open lines for our pieces. If White takes on e5, we recapture with the knight, gaining activity. This move also prepares to free our bishop on g7 and creates a pawn chain that restricts White's pieces.
ideas.shortText: e5 challenges the center and opens lines.

ideas.text: Nh3 develops the knight to a somewhat unusual square, but it's aimed at f4 and g5, supporting White's kingside plans. However, this knight is awkwardly placed and can become a target. We'll use this to our advantage as we continue our own development.
ideas.shortText: Nh3 is an awkward but purposeful development.

ideas.text: Nge7 brings our knight to a flexible square, eyeing f5 and d5. It also clears the way for our bishop on g7 to have more influence. We're now fully developed and ready to strike in the center or on the kingside, depending on White's next move.
ideas.shortText: Nge7 completes our development, eyeing f5.

d6.label: Carlsen Variation
d6.teaser: d6 sets the stage for a closed Sicilian battle, where we'll fight for control of the center and prepare a kingside clamp.

ideas.text: d4 strikes at the heart of Black's setup. We're challenging the c5 pawn immediately, forcing Black to make a decision about the center. This is the classic break that defines the Open Sicilian, and here it's especially potent because Black's knight on c3 is already committed, limiting their flexibility.
ideas.shortText: d4 — the central challenge.

ideas.text: cxd4 — Black accepts the trade, and now we have a choice. Instead of recapturing with the knight, we bring the queen out with Qxd4. This might look unusual, but it's a precise move: it keeps the knight on c3 free to develop, and it puts pressure on the d6 pawn, which is now a bit weak without its neighbor on c5.
ideas.shortText: cxd4 — we recapture with the queen.

ideas.text: Qxd4 — the queen steps into the center, but this is not just a greedy grab. It's a move that fights for control of the d-file and the dark squares. Black's next move, Nc6, will attack the queen, but we're ready to retreat to a safe square while keeping our central influence.
ideas.shortText: Qxd4 — centralizing the queen.

ideas.text: Nc6 — Black develops with tempo, attacking our queen. This is a natural move, but it also signals that Black is happy to trade off central pawns and play a more open game. We need to be careful not to let the queen get chased around, but we have a good retreat planned.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 — Black attacks the queen.

ideas.text: Qd2 — the queen drops back, but this is not a retreat in shame. It's a flexible square that keeps an eye on the center and prepares to connect the rooks. Notice how we've kept the knight on c3 and the bishop on f1 free to develop. Black's central pawns are gone, but we have a lead in development and a clear plan to build up pressure.
ideas.shortText: Qd2 — a flexible retreat.

richter veresov attack.intro: This line is all about one thing: White's dream of playing e4. Every move we make either supports that dream or punishes Black for trying to stop it. Watch how a single pawn push can turn the whole game on its head.
richter veresov attack.shortIntro: The battle for e4 defines this opening.
richter veresov attack.outro: And that's the story of the Richter-Veresov: a single-minded push for e4, and the precise way Black can dismantle it. Remember, when your opponent makes a weakening move like f3, strike in the center—c5 is the key. Keep this pattern in mind, and you'll be ready for anyone who tries to get too creative against d4.

ideas.text: We start with d4, claiming our share of the center and opening lines for the queen and bishop. This is the foundation of everything we want to do—it's the pawn that will become the target of Black's counterplay, but for now, it's the anchor of our space advantage.
ideas.shortText: d4 stakes our claim in the center.

ideas.text: Black answers with Nf6, developing a knight and putting immediate pressure on our d4 pawn. This is the most flexible reply—it keeps all options open and invites us to commit to a plan. Notice how Black is already eyeing the e4 square, ready to fight for it.
ideas.shortText: Nf6 pressures d4 and eyes e4.

ideas.text: Nc3 is the move that gives this opening its character. It develops the knight to its most active square, but it also blocks our c-pawn. That's a trade-off we accept because it supports the big idea: pushing e4. The knight on c3 is the battering ram that will help us break through in the center.
ideas.shortText: Nc3 supports the e4 push.

ideas.text: Black plays d5, and this is the critical moment. By challenging our d4 pawn, Black is saying, 'If you want e4, you'll have to work for it.' This move prevents e4 for now, because after e4, Black can simply take on e4 and we'd have to recapture with the knight, giving up the center. So we need a different way to fight for that square.
ideas.shortText: d5 challenges our center and blocks e4.

ideas.text: Bg5 is our response—a pin that increases the pressure on the knight and prepares to castle quickly. The bishop on g5 also eyes the e7 square, and it sets a trap: if Black is careless, we can take on f6 and double their pawns, weakening their kingside. But the real point is to keep the tension and make Black prove that d5 was the right move.
ideas.shortText: Bg5 pins the knight and prepares castling.

ideas.text: Black develops the light-squared bishop to f5, eyeing the e4 square. This is a natural developing move that also puts pressure on the center. However, it doesn't actually stop White from playing e4—White can still push the pawn and sacrifice it, leading to a sharp position where Black's bishop on f5 becomes a target. The bishop is not safe here; it can be hit by e4, and after the dust settles, White's queen can come to f3 with tempo, attacking the bishop and creating chaos. So while Bf5 is a reasonable move, it's not the most precise—Black should be looking for a way to strike at White's center immediately, rather than allowing White to take the initiative.
ideas.shortText: Bf5 is natural but allows e4, so Black should strike the center first.

ideas.text: White plays f3, a move that looks like it's preparing e4, but it's a double-edged sword. On one hand, it supports the e4 push and gives White a solid center. On the other hand, it weakens the kingside and, crucially, takes away the f3 square from the knight, making it harder to defend the d4 pawn. This is a key moment: Black should recognize that White's f3 is a concession—it's a move that doesn't develop and creates weaknesses. Black can now exploit this by playing c5, striking at the center and putting pressure on d4, since White can no longer bring the knight to f3 to help defend it. This is the beginning of Black's plan to undermine White's center and expose the weaknesses created by f3.
ideas.shortText: f3 weakens the kingside and blocks the knight, so Black should strike with c5.

sicilian defense accelerated dragon.intro: This is the Accelerated Dragon, and the whole game is about one square: d4. White's early c4 has created a permanent hole on d4 that we'll spend the entire opening fighting over. But here's the key lesson — controlling a square and occupying it are two different things. We're going to be patient, develop our pieces, and only later will we cash in on that weakness.
sicilian defense accelerated dragon.shortIntro: The Accelerated Dragon: fight for d4, but don't rush to occupy it.
sicilian defense accelerated dragon.outro: And that's the Accelerated Dragon in a nutshell: don't rush to plant a knight on d4. Instead, build a wall of pieces and pawns that controls the square from afar, trade off the defenders, and only then occupy it. The hole doesn't go away — it just waits for the right moment.

ideas.text: e4 opens the center and stakes a claim to d4 and f5. White is saying, 'I'll control the center.' We respond in classic Sicilian fashion: we don't try to fight for the center symmetrically — we'll chip away from the flank.
ideas.shortText: e4: White claims the center; we'll fight from the flank.

ideas.text: c5 stakes our claim to the d4 hole. White's e-pawn and c-pawn have both advanced to the fourth rank, so neither can defend a square on that rank anymore — d4 is a permanent weakness. We're not going to jump a knight in right away, though; that would just let White kick it out. The hole is a long-term asset, and we'll build toward it.
ideas.shortText: c5 claims the d4 hole for later.

ideas.text: White develops the knight to f3, bringing another piece to bear on our d4 outpost. But here's the thing: we're not in a hurry to jump a knight to d4 ourselves. That square is a long-term weakness for white—it's not going anywhere. What matters is that we keep control of it from afar, and that's exactly what our next move will set up.
ideas.shortText: Nf3 eyes d4, but we're not rushing—control matters more.

ideas.text: Nc6 develops a knight and puts pressure on d4, but we're not planning to jump to d4 immediately. If we played Nd4 now, White would just play Nf3 and kick our knight away. The hole is a long-term asset, not a short-term target. We develop naturally and keep the d4 square in our sights.
ideas.shortText: Nc6: Develop, but don't rush to d4.

ideas.text: d4 is White's attempt to close the hole, but it doesn't work — it just gives us a target. When White pushes d4, we take with our c-pawn, and the hole moves to a different square: now it's the d4 pawn itself that's weak, and White's knight will have to recapture. This is exactly the kind of central tension we want.
ideas.shortText: d4 opens the center; we take.

ideas.text: cxd4 removes White's pawn and leaves the d4 square empty again. Now White's knight is forced to recapture, which means it leaves its natural square on f3. We're happy to let White centralize a piece here because our plan is to challenge it later. The hole is still there — it's just wearing a different uniform.
ideas.shortText: cxd4 clears d4 for our knight.

ideas.text: Nxd4 puts a knight on the hole, but this is not the moment to celebrate. White's knight is well-placed, but it's also a target. Our next move will start the process of undermining it. The key is that we're not going to let this knight stay — we'll trade it off or chase it away, and then the hole becomes ours.
ideas.shortText: Nxd4 occupies the hole — for now.

ideas.text: Now we fianchetto with g6. This is the defining move of the Accelerated Dragon: we're preparing to post our bishop on the long diagonal, where it will exert immense pressure on the center and especially on the d4 square. By keeping the pawn on d7, we retain the option to strike with d5 later—a key resource that the mainline Dragon doesn't have. This is the move that gives our whole setup its character.
ideas.shortText: g6 prepares the fianchetto, keeping d5 in reserve.

Nc3.text: Everything up to this point is the same road you already own—the Accelerated Dragon's early moves. The main continuation, c4, locks the center with the Maróczy Bind, aiming to cramp us and build a slow squeeze. Today's sideline, Nc3, instead develops a knight and keeps the center fluid, inviting us to fianchetto and strike with d5. Watch how the fight for the d5 square becomes the central theme as this line unfolds.
Nc3.shortText: c4 locks the center; Nc3 keeps it fluid.
Nc3.textFlipped: Everything up to this point is the same road you already own—the Accelerated Dragon's early moves. The main continuation, c4, locks the center with the Maróczy Bind, aiming to cramp Black and build a slow squeeze. Today's sideline, Nc3, instead develops a knight and keeps the center fluid, inviting Black to fianchetto and strike with d5. Watch how the fight for the d5 square becomes the central theme as this line unfolds.
Nc3.shortTextFlipped: c4 locks the center; Nc3 keeps it fluid.

Nxc6.text: Everything up to this moment is the same road you already own—the Accelerated Dragon's early moves are yours. But now the path splits: the main continuation plays c4, locking the center with the Maróczy Bind, aiming to restrict your pieces and build a space advantage. Today's sideline, Nxc6, takes a different route—it trades off your knight, opening the b-file and preparing to push e5, trying to seize central space with pawns. Watch how your pawn structure and piece activity change as this new line unfolds.
Nxc6.shortText: Main c4 locks the center; sideline Nxc6 opens the b-file.

Nc3.label: Modern Variation
Nc3.teaser: Nc3 is the most natural way for White to develop, but it also signals that they're not afraid of the Accelerated Dragon. Now we get to show why this opening is so dangerous: our dark-squared bishop is about to take aim at the long diagonal.
Nc3.shortTeaser: Nc3 develops, but our bishop is ready to dominate the dark squares.

ideas.text: Bg7 finishes the fianchetto, and now the bishop on g7 is the star of our position. It controls the long diagonal, putting pressure on the d4 knight and the b2 pawn. This is the piece that will make White's life miserable if they don't respect it.
ideas.shortText: Bg7: our bishop eyes the long diagonal, pressuring d4 and b2.

ideas.text: Be3 is White's most natural way to develop, but it also creates a target. Notice that the bishop on e3 is now on the same diagonal as our g7 bishop, and it's a piece we can attack with tempo later. For now, we just continue with our own development.
ideas.shortText: Be3 develops, but it's a target for our bishop later.

ideas.text: Nf6 is the key move in this position. We're not just developing a piece; we're preparing to challenge White's center with d5. The knight on f6 also eyes the e4 pawn, which is a constant thorn in White's side. If White ever plays f3 to support e4, we'll have d5 ready to strike.
ideas.shortText: Nf6: preparing d5 to break the center.

ideas.text: Bc4 is a natural developing move for White, but it also allows us to play d5 immediately. The bishop on c4 is a target for our pawn break, and if White takes on d5, we recapture with the knight, gaining a tempo on the bishop. This is the moment our preparation pays off.
ideas.shortText: Bc4: now d5 is even stronger, hitting the bishop.

Nxc6.label: Exchange Variation
Nxc6.teaser: Nxc6 — the Exchange Variation. White trades our knight to open the b-file and challenge our dark-square grip. We'll recapture toward the center and turn that open file into our highway.
Nxc6.shortTeaser: Nxc6 — the Exchange Variation. We recapture toward the center and use the open b-file.

sicilian defense nyezhmetdinov rossolimo.openingName: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Gurgenidze Variation
sicilian defense nyezhmetdinov rossolimo.intro: The Rossolimo is a positional beast: White trades a bishop for a knight to damage Black's pawn structure, then spends the whole game exploiting those cracks. The battle is over the d4-square and the weak pawns on c6 and a6 — every move we make should either tighten our grip on the center or point at those targets.
sicilian defense nyezhmetdinov rossolimo.shortIntro: A positional fight: White trades a bishop to damage Black's pawns, then squeezes the center.
sicilian defense nyezhmetdinov rossolimo.outro: The bishop trade has done its job: Black's pawns are cracked, and our pieces are already circling the weak squares. Now we develop with purpose, keeping the center solid and the pressure on — the rest of the game is about turning this structural edge into a win.

ideas.text: e4 stakes a claim in the center, opening lines for the bishop and queen. It's the first step in a battle for control of the key squares, especially d4 and d5.
ideas.shortText: e4 grabs central space and opens lines.

ideas.text: c5 is the Sicilian's signature: Black immediately challenges the e4 pawn and fights for the d4 square. This move sets up a pawn structure that will define the fight for the center.
ideas.shortText: c5 challenges e4 and fights for d4.

ideas.text: Nf3 develops and eyes the e5-square, but more importantly it clears the way for our bishop to reach b5. This knight is a quiet piece — it's not attacking anything yet, but it's part of the setup that lets us trade on c6 and start chipping at Black's pawns.
ideas.shortText: Nf3 prepares the bishop's journey to b5.

ideas.text: Nc6 is Black's natural development, but it walks right into our plan. The knight is a target — we're going to trade our bishop for it, and Black will have to recapture with a pawn, leaving doubled c-pawns and a hole on c6. That's the structural damage we're after.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 is the target — we'll trade bishop for knight.

ideas.text: Bb5 is the Rossolimo: White develops the bishop to b5, eyeing the knight on c6. The idea is to pressure Black's structure and, if Black takes, recapture with the d-pawn to open lines and control the center.
ideas.shortText: Bb5 pressures the knight and prepares central control.

ideas.text: With g6, Black commits to the fianchetto setup. This is the Accelerated Dragon's answer to the Rossolimo — we're signaling that we'll develop the bishop to g7 and fight for the center with pieces rather than pawns. It's a flexible move that keeps all options open, but it also tells White we're not afraid of the bishop pair.
ideas.shortText: g6 commits to the fianchetto, the Accelerated Dragon's answer to the Rossolimo.

ideas.text: O-O is the natural follow-up. Now that our king is safe, we can focus on the center. Notice that White hasn't committed to taking on c6 yet — that's fine, we're just developing and keeping our structure intact. Castling also prepares to bring the rook to e1, which will support the e4 pawn and eye the center.
ideas.shortText: O-O gets the king safe, ready for central operations.

ideas.text: Bg7 completes the fianchetto. This bishop is the star of our setup — it controls the long diagonal and puts pressure on d4. With the bishop on g7, we're clamping down on the dark squares, making it hard for White to play d4 without consequences. This is the classic Accelerated Dragon idea: fight for the center with pieces, not just pawns.
ideas.shortText: Bg7 finishes the fianchetto, clamping down on d4.

ideas.text: Re1 is a precise move. Instead of committing to c3 or d4 immediately, White keeps the center flexible. The rook on e1 supports the e4 pawn and prepares to push d4 in one go. It also discourages ...Bg4, since the bishop would be hitting a defended pawn. This is a waiting move — White wants to see our setup before choosing the plan.
ideas.shortText: Re1 supports e4 and keeps d4 as a future option.

ideas.text: e5 is the key move. This is the defining decision of the Gurgenidze Variation. By pushing the pawn to e5, we lock the center and create a clamp on d4. The bishop on g7 and the pawn on e5 work together as a unit, controlling the key squares. This move also frees the knight to go to e7, where it will support the center and prepare a kingside pawn storm. It looks like it blocks the bishop, but in this structure, the bishop and pawn are a team — the pawn is an extension of the bishop's power.
ideas.shortText: e5 locks the center, clamping down on d4.

ideas.text: b4 is a space-gaining move on the queenside, but it's also about supporting the central clamp. White is grabbing room to maneuver and preparing to reinforce the d4 square, keeping Black's pieces passive.
ideas.shortText: b4 gains space and supports the center.

torre attack classical defense.intro: The Torre Attack looks like a London System, but that bishop on g5 changes everything. In this line, White's real challenge is to make something of the pin while Black tries to prove that the bishop is misplaced. We'll see how the fight for the center and the dark squares shapes the whole game.
torre attack classical defense.shortIntro: The Torre Attack: a London lookalike with a twist—the bishop on g5 changes everything.
torre attack classical defense.outro: So there you have it: the Torre Attack is not just a London with a different bishop square—it's a completely different animal. The pin on the knight is the key, and Black must be careful not to let White's pressure build. Remember, the battle for the center and the dark squares will decide who comes out on top.

ideas.text: We start with d4, claiming a big share of the center and opening lines for the queen and bishop. It's the foundation of every queen pawn opening, and here it sets the stage for the battle over the dark squares.
ideas.shortText: d4 stakes our claim in the center.

ideas.text: Black answers with Nf6, developing and immediately attacking our pawn. This is the most natural reply—it puts pressure on d4 and prepares to control the center with e6 or d5.
ideas.shortText: Nf6 challenges our center right away.

ideas.text: We bring out the knight to f3, defending d4 and preparing to castle. It's a quiet move, but it keeps our options open—we could go for the London with Bf4, or the Torre with Bg5, or even a kingside fianchetto.
ideas.shortText: Nf3 supports d4 and keeps our plans flexible.

ideas.text: Black plays e6, solidifying the center and freeing the light-squared bishop. This is a flexible move—it could lead to a French or a Queen's Indian, but here it sets up the classical defense to the Torre.
ideas.shortText: e6 shores up Black's center and frees the bishop.

ideas.text: Now we play Bg5, pinning the knight on f6. This is the defining move of the Torre Attack—it looks like the London, but the bishop on g5 puts pressure on Black's position. The pin makes it hard for Black to play e5, and it sets up the possibility of trading on f6 to damage Black's kingside.
ideas.shortText: Bg5 pins the knight and defines the Torre.

c5.label: Petrosian Gambit
c5.teaser: Black answers with c5, striking at the center and signaling the Petrosian Gambit — a flexible, counterattacking setup.
c5.shortTeaser: c5 — Black strikes the center, inviting the Petrosian Gambit.

ideas.text: With e3, White shores up the d4 pawn and keeps the position solid, but it's a modest move that doesn't challenge Black's setup.
ideas.shortText: e3 — solid, but unambitious.

ideas.text: Black's b6 prepares to fianchetto the bishop, adding pressure on d4 and the long diagonal — a typical idea in this gambit.
ideas.shortText: b6 — preparing the fianchetto.

ideas.text: d5 is the point: Black strikes in the center, and if White takes, Black recaptures with the queen, gaining free play and a lead in development.
ideas.shortText: d5 — the central strike.

modern defense.intro: This line is all about the fight for the center and the light squares. Black's Modern Defense with g6 and Nh6 is a tricky setup, but we're going to meet it with principled play, aiming to control the center and exploit Black's unusual knight development.
modern defense.shortIntro: Black's Modern Defense: we fight for the center and punish the early Nh6.
modern defense.outro: With our pieces developed and the center secured, we're ready to continue our plan. Black's knight on h6 is misplaced, and our control of the center gives us a solid advantage.

ideas.text: e4 stakes our claim in the center immediately. Black's g6 signals the Modern Defense, a flexible setup where they delay committing their knight. By occupying the center, we dare them to challenge it.
ideas.shortText: e4 grabs the center, challenging Black's flexible Modern.

ideas.text: Black starts with g6, the Modern Defense. This is a flexible setup where Black delays knight development, keeping options open for a Pirc or a Gurgenidze. We need to be ready to play principled chess against it.
ideas.shortText: Black plays g6, the Modern Defense, staying flexible.

ideas.text: d4 grabs space and stakes a claim in the center. White is saying, 'I'll take the center, you try to undermine it.' This is the principled response to Black's provocative setup, and it sets the stage for the coming battle over the dark squares.
ideas.shortText: d4: White seizes central space.

ideas.text: Nh6 is Black's attempt to reroute the knight to f5, but it leaves the knight on the rim, where it's not doing much. We'll develop naturally and look to punish this misplaced piece.
ideas.shortText: Nh6 is a rim job; we'll punish it.

ideas.text: Nc3 develops and supports our d4 pawn. It also prepares to meet Black's ...d5 with exd5, transposing into a favorable Fantasy-like structure. Our pieces are coming out with purpose, while Black's knight is stuck on h6.
ideas.shortText: Nc3 develops and eyes the center.

ideas.text: f5 is a bold pawn thrust, but it's premature. Black is opening the center while White has a lead in development, which is exactly what you shouldn't do. This move creates a permanent weakness on e6 and gives White a target to attack.
ideas.shortText: f5: Black opens the center prematurely.

ideas.text: Bxh6 is a key move: White trades off Black's dark-squared bishop, the piece that was supposed to control the long diagonal. This leaves Black with a gaping hole on h6 and weakens the dark squares around Black's king. It's a clear signal that White is going for the attack.
ideas.shortText: Bxh6: White removes Black's key defender.

ideas.text: Black recaptures with Bxh6, but this bishop is not the same piece it was on g7. Now it's on h6, where it's actually a bit awkward — it's not doing much, and our dark-squared bishop is gone, but we still have a nice grip on the center. The key is that we're not in a hurry; we can continue developing and building pressure.
ideas.shortText: Black's bishop ends up misplaced on h6 — we're fine.

ideas.text: exf5 opens the f-file and gives White a protected passed pawn on f5. This pawn cramps Black's position and serves as a battering ram for the kingside attack. White is not just winning a pawn; they're creating a permanent structural advantage.
ideas.shortText: exf5: White gains a powerful passer.

ideas.text: O-O gets the king to safety and connects the rooks. Now White can double on the f-file or bring the rook to e1, increasing the pressure. Black's king is still in the center, and White's pieces are ready to swarm.
ideas.shortText: O-O: White's king finds safety.

bishop s opening.intro: This line is all about the fight for the f-file. White's early f4 gambit aims to open it, but Black's solid setup turns that very file into a weapon. Every move here is a step in that battle — who controls the f-file, and what they do with it.
bishop s opening.shortIntro: The battle for the f-file defines this line.
bishop s opening.outro: And that's the story of the f-file — White tried to pry it open, but Black's solid setup turned it into a highway to the king. The gambit pawns come back with interest, and White's position collapses under the pressure.

ideas.text: e4 opens the center and stakes a claim to the d5 and f5 squares. It's the first step in a fight for space, and it sets the stage for the bishop to come out next.
ideas.shortText: e4 grabs central space and prepares the bishop.

ideas.text: e5 answers in kind — Black mirrors the central claim, and now the board is set for a classic open game. White's next move will aim at the f7 square, the weakest point in Black's camp.
ideas.shortText: e5 keeps the center balanced.

ideas.text: Bc4 is the Bishop's Opening — White develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, pointing straight at f7. It's a natural developing move, but it also sets a subtle trap: if Black isn't careful, the bishop can become a monster on that diagonal.
ideas.shortText: Bc4 targets f7, the classic weak point.

ideas.text: Bc5 is Black's natural reply — they develop the bishop to the same kind of active square, eyeing f2. Now both sides have their bishops aimed at the opponent's weakest pawn, and the tension is set.
ideas.shortText: Bc5 mirrors White's bishop, eyeing f2.

ideas.text: b4 is the gambit — White offers a pawn to deflect the bishop and gain time. The idea is to lure the bishop away from the a7-g1 diagonal, but it also weakens the c4 square and gives Black a target. It's a double-edged move that sets the tone for the whole line.
ideas.shortText: b4 is the gambit — a pawn for time and disruption.

ideas.text: Bxb4 accepts the gift — Black takes the pawn and calls White's bluff. Now White has to prove the gambit is worth it, but Black's bishop is well-placed on b4, and the extra pawn is real. The f-file battle is about to begin.
ideas.shortText: Bxb4 grabs the pawn and challenges the gambit.

ideas.text: f4 is the point — White strikes at the center and opens the f-file. This is the move that gives the gambit its character: if Black takes, the file opens, and White hopes to use it for an attack. But as we'll see, that file can cut both ways.
ideas.shortText: f4 opens the f-file — the gambit's core idea.

ideas.text: exf4 takes the pawn and opens the f-file — but now Black has a clear path down that file. White's king is still in the center, and the open file is a highway for Black's rooks. The gambit has backfired: White's attack is blunted, and Black's counterplay is born.
ideas.shortText: exf4 opens the file — but for Black's benefit.

ideas.text: Nf3 develops the knight and prepares to recapture the f4 pawn. It also guards the h4 square, but the knight on f3 is a target — Black will soon show how to exploit that. For now, it's a natural developing move, but it's also a piece that can become a liability.
ideas.shortText: Nf3 develops and eyes the f4 pawn.

ideas.text: Be7 is the solid choice. Black declines the sharp Italian lines and keeps the position closed, but the f-file is already half-open, and White will look to use it.
ideas.shortText: Be7 keeps it solid, but the f-file is open.

ideas.text: d4 strikes in the center. With the f-pawn gone, White opens lines and prepares to bring the rook to the f-file, increasing the pressure.
ideas.shortText: d4 opens lines for the rook.

ideas.text: Black's bishop slides to h4, giving check and maintaining the pin on our knight. This is a critical moment: we must respond accurately, because allowing the pin to persist would let Black dominate the center and keep our king stuck.
ideas.shortText: Bh4+ keeps the pin; we must react precisely.

ideas.text: g3 is the only way to break the pin and chase the bishop away. By attacking it with a pawn, we force Black to make a decision — and whatever he chooses, we're ready to open the f-file and launch our own attack.
ideas.shortText: g3 attacks the bishop and frees our position.

ideas.text: fxg3 recaptures with the pawn, keeping the f-file open and maintaining the attack. The pawn on g3 also gives White's king a shelter.
ideas.shortText: fxg3 keeps the f-file open.

ideas.text: O-O is the key move: we tuck our king away and bring the rook to the f-file, which is now half-open. This is the payoff of our earlier pawn breaks — we have a clear path to attack Black's king, while our own is safe.
ideas.shortText: O-O secures our king and activates the rook.

ideas.text: Black's pawn storms to h2, giving check and opening the h-file even further. This looks scary, but it's actually a gift: our king can step aside, and the pawn on h2 becomes a permanent weakness that we can target.
ideas.shortText: gxh2+ opens the h-file; our king steps aside.

ideas.text: Kh1 sidesteps the check and completes our king's journey to safety. Now Black's pawn on h2 is stuck, and we have a clear path to attack down the h-file — our pieces are ready to deliver the final blow.
ideas.shortText: Kh1 escapes check and leaves Black's pawn stranded.

queen s gambit accepted.intro: This line is all about the fight for the d4-pawn and the center. White gambits a pawn to build a powerful pawn center and seize the initiative, while black tries to hold onto the extra pawn and undermine white's structure. The tension revolves around whether white can maintain the center and develop with tempo, or whether black can consolidate and neutralize white's space advantage.
queen s gambit accepted.shortIntro: White gambits a pawn to build a powerful center and seize the initiative.
queen s gambit accepted.outro: With the knight on f3, white has developed a piece and prepared to recapture the pawn on c4. The battle for the center continues, with white's space advantage and black's extra pawn hanging in the balance. The next moves will determine whether white can maintain the initiative or black can consolidate.

ideas.text: We start with d4, staking a claim in the center and opening lines for our pieces. This is the first step in building a strong pawn center, which will be the foundation of our play.
ideas.shortText: d4 claims the center and opens lines.

ideas.text: Black responds with d5, directly challenging our central pawn. This is a natural move, but it sets the stage for the tension that will define the opening.
ideas.shortText: Black challenges our center with d5.

ideas.text: Now we play c4, the Queen's Gambit. We offer a pawn to deflect black's d5 pawn and gain more control over the center. If black takes, we'll have a lead in development and a strong center to build on.
ideas.shortText: c4 offers a pawn to gain central control.

ideas.text: Black accepts the gambit with dxc4, taking the pawn. This is the Queen's Gambit Accepted. Black grabs material but falls behind in development. Our job now is to recapture the pawn while maintaining our central presence and initiative.
ideas.shortText: Black takes the pawn, accepting the gambit.

ideas.text: We develop the knight to f3, preparing to recapture the pawn on c4 with our bishop. This also adds pressure on d4 and e5, and gets a piece out while keeping our options open for the center.
ideas.shortText: Nf3 develops and prepares to recapture.

ideas.text: Nf6 develops the knight to its most natural square, attacking nothing but preparing to castle. It's a solid developing move that keeps the position flexible.
ideas.shortText: Nf6 develops and prepares to castle.

ideas.text: We play e3, and this is the calm, positional choice. Instead of trying to blow black off the board with e4, we're saying, 'I'll just win the pawn back and build a solid center.' The downside is that our bishop on c1 is now blocked, but we're prioritizing safety and structure over immediate aggression.
ideas.shortText: e3 is the solid, positional way to reclaim the pawn.

ideas.text: e6 solidifies the center and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop. It's a quiet but important move, ensuring Black's pawn structure remains sound.
ideas.shortText: e6 solidifies the center.

ideas.text: Now we take back the pawn with Bxc4. This is the moment we've been working toward: we've regained our pawn, and our bishop is now on a great diagonal, eyeing f7. Black's position is solid, but we have a slight space advantage, and our pieces are ready to flow out. The battle will revolve around the d5 square—if we can control it, black will be in trouble.
ideas.shortText: Bxc4 recaptures the pawn and eyes f7.

ideas.text: Black plays c5, striking at our center immediately. This is the critical test: if we allow black to trade on d4, we'll end up with an isolated pawn, which can be a weakness. But we're not afraid—we can simply castle, and then we'll have a comfortable game. The key is to remember that our center is solid, and we have no weaknesses to exploit.
ideas.shortText: c5 challenges our center, but we're ready.

ideas.text: Now we castle, getting the king to safety and connecting the rooks. Black's counterplay is gone — our king was the last loose end, and with it tied up, our extra pawn and better development will do the rest.
ideas.shortText: Castle to safety; the rest is easy.

owen defense.intro: This line is all about the fight for the e4 pawn. Black's bishop on b7 is eyeing it, and the whole opening is built around overprotecting that pawn so Black's pressure never becomes a real threat. We're going to see how a simple setup can neutralize Black's ideas and leave us with a comfortable, active position.
owen defense.outro: With the bishop on d3, we've overprotected e4 and taken the sting out of Black's pressure. The stage is set for a comfortable game where Black's bishop on b7 is just a spectator.

ideas.text: White opens with e4, claiming the center and inviting us to react. But we're not here to play a normal game — we're going to let White overextend, then strike at the weak points. Our b6 is the first step in a plan to make White's center a target, not a strength.
ideas.shortText: White claims the center; we'll let them overextend and strike back.

ideas.text: Black responds with b6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop to b7. That bishop is going to put pressure on e4, so we need to be ready to defend it properly.
ideas.shortText: b6 signals the bishop is coming to b7.

ideas.text: d4 grabs the center and opens lines for the queen and bishop. It's the natural follow-up to b6, claiming space and preparing to develop quickly. White is already eyeing the e4 pawn, which becomes a target for Black's pieces.
ideas.shortText: d4 claims central space and prepares development.

ideas.text: There it is: Bb7, the point of b6. That bishop is now staring down the long diagonal at e4. It's a good move, but we have a plan to make it harmless.
ideas.shortText: Bb7 puts pressure on e4.

ideas.text: Bd3 is the key move. We overprotect e4, so Black's pressure on that pawn is neutralized. The bishop also has potential energy, aiming at the kingside if Black ever castles. This is the foundation of our whole setup.
ideas.shortText: Bd3 overprotects e4 and eyes the kingside.

ideas.text: Black strikes at the heart of our setup with f5, challenging the e4 pawn and trying to open lines for the bishop on b7. This is the Owen's Defense's main counterpunch — if we let Black take on e4, our center crumbles. But we're ready: our pieces are overprotecting e4, so this pawn break doesn't scare us. Instead, we see it as an invitation to open the position and expose Black's uncastled king.
ideas.shortText: f5 challenges our center, but our pieces are ready to punish.

ideas.text: exf5 captures the pawn and opens the f-file, but it also gives Black's bishop on b7 a clear diagonal. This trade simplifies the center and leaves White with a pawn on f5, which can be a target. The move is straightforward, but it changes the character of the position.
ideas.shortText: exf5 opens the f-file and simplifies the center.

ideas.text: Black grabs the pawn back with Bxg2, snatching material and attacking our rook on h1. This is a critical moment — we can't let Black get away with this. But notice: Black's bishop on g2 is now far from the action, and our queen is ready to leap into the attack. We have a lead in development and a clear plan: use our pieces to hunt down Black's king before they can consolidate.
ideas.shortText: Bxg2 wins a pawn, but Black's king is still exposed.

ideas.text: Qh5+ is the hammer blow — we check the king and force it to move, keeping the initiative. Black's king has no safe square: it can't go to e7 because our bishop on d3 controls that, and it can't stay on e8 because we'll just keep checking. This is the payoff for all our development — Black's pieces are still on their starting squares, and we're already attacking with our queen.
ideas.shortText: Qh5+ forces the king out, exploiting Black's lag.

ideas.text: Black tries to block the check with g6, but this only weakens the dark squares around their king. Now we have a target: the pawn on g6 is a hook we can use to open the king side. Our next moves will be about breaking through — maybe with a pawn push or a piece sacrifice — while Black's king remains trapped in the center. The attack is just beginning.
ideas.shortText: g6 weakens the king side, giving us a target.

vienna game copycat variation.intro: Black is going to copy us move for move, and the question this whole line answers is: when does copying stop working? The answer is the first move that only works for one of us — and we are going to find it, on g7.
vienna game copycat variation.shortIntro: When does copying stop working? On g7.
vienna game copycat variation.outro: Play it again and watch g7 from move one.

ideas.text: e4. The centre, and the diagonal the queen and the bishop both want. Nothing controversial yet — but everything in this line comes from one square, f7, and the pieces that will end up pointing at it.
ideas.shortText: e4 — the centre, and the road to f7.

ideas.text: Black mirrors. That is the whole idea we are about to test: copying is comfortable, it never loses a tempo, and it works right up until the position stops being symmetrical.
ideas.shortText: e5 — the mirror begins.

ideas.text: The knight comes to c3, holding e4 and keeping the king's knight at home so we still get to choose where it goes. Quiet, and deliberately non-committal.
ideas.shortText: Nc3 holds e4 and keeps our options.

ideas.text: Black copies again, and here the mirror starts costing something. The knight on c6 is a perfectly good square — but it is not f6, and f6 is the square that guards g7. Nobody notices that for another three moves.
ideas.shortText: Nc6 mirrors, but leaves f6 empty.

ideas.text: The bishop takes the long diagonal and points at f7 — the one square the king alone defends. Still nothing forced. We are just arranging the pieces that will ask the question.
ideas.shortText: Bc4 aims at f7.

ideas.text: And the mirror is complete. Black has copied every move and the position is dead level — which is exactly why this is worth learning, because from here the copying has to stop and Black usually does not know when. Two queen moves are close to equal here; the one we want is the one that asks about g7.
ideas.shortText: Bc5 — the copycat, and level.

ideas.text: Out comes the queen, straight at g7. Count the defenders of that pawn: there are none. The knight that would normally cover it went to c6 instead, and that is the bill for four moves of copying. Black cannot copy this one — the same move for him hangs everything.
ideas.shortText: Qg4 — g7 has no defender.

ideas.text: Black defends g7 with the queen, which looks like the natural answer and is the moment the game turns. Before this the position was level; now it is clearly better for us. Defending with the queen puts it on a square the whole board can shout at.
ideas.shortText: Qf6 defends g7 — and walks into it.

ideas.text: The knight jumps to d5 and hits the queen — and behind that, if the queen simply steps away, comes the fork on c7, check on the king and the rook in the corner. I love a move that asks two questions at once; Black can answer either, not both.
ideas.shortText: Nd5 hits the queen and eyes c7.

ideas.text: Black takes on f2 with check and grabs the pawn. Here is where a lot of players reach for the bishop instead — same square, same check, and it feels like the piece you would rather use. But the king steps to f1 and the bishop is simply sitting there attacked, with nothing to show for it. The queen is the one move that works.
ideas.shortText: Qxf2+ takes with check — not the bishop.

ideas.text: The king steps aside to d1. We have given up castling and we are not pretending otherwise — but the king is safe behind its own pawns, and Black's problem is about to be bigger than ours.
ideas.shortText: Kd1 — castling gone, king fine.

ideas.text: Black has to do the same, and that is the trade this whole line is built on: we both lose the right to castle, but our king walked to safety while theirs is stuck on f8 with the rook boxed in behind it. Offering the queen trade on e2 here would be the wrong instinct — Black takes it with check and the pressure evaporates.
ideas.shortText: Kf8 — both kings stuck, ours better.

ideas.text: The knight develops to h3 and, from that unlikely square, attacks the queen on f2. This is the move Black most often meets by developing the other knight to f6 — and that just loses the queen to the knight on h3. The queen has to move, and the clock has been running on it since it took the pawn.
ideas.shortText: Nh3 attacks the queen on f2.

ideas.text: The queen drops back to d4, and it is not running — from there it hits the bishop on c4, which nothing is defending, and the pawn on e4 as well. Two targets. This is Black's best try and it still does not solve the real problem.
ideas.shortText: Qd4 hits the bishop and e4.

ideas.text: d3, and both threats are answered at once — the pawn shields e4 and gives the bishop on c4 the defender it was missing. Now take stock: we are clearly better, close to two pawns' worth. Black has no castling, a king stuck on f8, a rook that cannot move, and a queen that has spent the whole game touring. That is the lesson of the copycat — mirroring is free until the first move that only works for one side, and then the bill arrives all at once.
ideas.shortText: d3 covers both — and we are much better.
